newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss businesses ready to add to Holocaust fund.
newsitem.headline: Swiss businesses ready to add to Holocaust fund.

text.p: Swiss business leaders are ready to contribute to a fund being set up by the country's three biggest banks in memory of Holocaust victims, the Swiss Foreign Ministry said on Sunday.

In a statement issued after Foreign Minister Flavio Cotti met business executives and Swiss National Bank officials here, the Foreign Ministry said the business chiefs indicated they were willing to add to the 100 million Swiss franc ($70 million) fund.

"On Sunday, top representatives of Swiss business and the National Bank met under the leadership of Minister Cotti. They carried out preliminary, general discussions pertaining to creation of a humanitarian fund. The representatives said that -- alongside the big banks -- the rest of industry is ready to contribute funds," a statement released by Cotti's office said.
"The Swiss cabinet will continue discussions with Jewish organisations and other groups with an interest in this matter in coming days," the statement said.
Thomas Borer, special ambassador in charge of coordinating Berne's response to Holocaust questions, said the meeting involved about a dozen Swiss industrialists.

Switzerland's three biggest banks, under fire from critics over their handling of Holocaust victims' bank accounts, pledged on February 5 to set aside 100 million Swiss francs for a Holocaust memorial fund.

Union Bank of Switzerland (UBS), Credit Suisse (CS) and Swiss Bank Corp (SBC) were reacting to allegations from Jewish organisations, Holocaust survivors and their families that Swiss banks hoarded assets of Holocaust victims placed with the banks for safekeeping during World War II.

The banks said they hoped creation of the fund would clear the way for the Swiss government, business and finance to work with Jewish organisations towards finding a "just and equitable solution" to the issues involved.
The Swiss National Bank also has been criticised by U.S. Senate Banking Committee Chairman Alfonse D'Amato over its role during World War II.

D'Amato, citing a 1946 document, said earlier this month that British, French and U.S. negotiators believed the Swiss were aware when they took in 100 tonnes of gold from Germany's wartime government that the gold was stolen from Belgium.
The Swiss central bank has said it was unclear if it knew at the time where the gold came from.

Some Swiss industrialists have been accused of helping the German war effort, or of being Nazi sympathisers. The Swiss press has also raised questions about Swiss insurers' handling of life insurance policies for Holocaust victims.
Swiss people have lately also raised questions about their country's treatment of Jewish refugees during the war.

The Swiss parliament is now weighing a proposal which would allow the government to pay out unclaimed bank accounts, including those left by Jews who died in the Holocaust. The money would be put into a fund which could be used by Jewish groups and charities.
